newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries extend losses amid more bearish data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries extend losses amid more bearish data.

text.p: For the second straight day, stronger-than-expected economic news sent prices of U.S. Treasuries tumbling and yields popping to levels not seen in more than two months.

At around midday Thursday, the 30-year bond was at 96-27/32, down 1-9/32 from late Tuesday. Its yield jumped to 6.746 percent from 6.64 percent, its highest level on a closing basis since 6.84 percent on October 28.
The two-year note, meanwhile, was down 5/32 at 99-19/32, to yield 5.969 percent. The yield had risen as high as 5.97 percent, which hasn't been seen since October 10.
Treasuries came off their lows around midday, as the sell-off made bonds more attractive, players noted. Still, there is more room on the downside than the upside, traders said.

"The market has had to digest two of these in a row," said a trader at a primary dealership, referring to surprisingly strong economic data both Tuesday and Thursday. "The market is repricing itself. The market has to consider that the Federal Reserve -- as remote a chance as it is -- will (raise rates) at its February meeting."

The latest shift in sentiment came as the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) reported that its December manufacturing index rose to 54.0 from 52.7 in November, its highest reading since June. The market had anticipated a reading of 51.5.
The prices index soared to 51.5 in December from 45.9 in November.

"The NAPM was what scared us, especially the price number was so large," said Craig Coats, co-head of taxable fixed income trading at Prudential Securities Inc. He added, however, that it is possible energy played a big part in the price gain.
The rise in the NAPM follows a huge jump in new home sales in November reported on Tuesday, which also triggered a one-point-plus sell-off.

Treasuries, though, began the session on a positive note, after the Labor Department reported that initial jobless claims rose to 366,000 in the week ended December 28 from a revised 344,000 in the prior week.

Treasury prices had risen as much as 3/8-point on the claims numbers, but started to edge back down just ahead of the NAPM report, along with a selloff in stocks. The Dow Jones Industrial index fell nearly 100 points, but has since recovered and was down about 50 points at 1233 EST/1733 GMT.

Then, immediately after the NAPM, Treasury prices fell faster than confetti in New York's Times Square on New Year's Eve. Traders said much of the selling was from hedge funds and other retail accounts.
"A lot of longs were dislodged from the market," said one trader.
Liquidity remains low, but volume was heavy during the selling spree, traders said. As such, some said it might take until next week until true levels can can be established.

For now, traders are looking for yields to continue rising. After moving up 40 basis points over the past month, players see the long bond climbing above 6.80 percent to a high of around 6.85 percent in the near term. Similarly, traders eye 6.0 percent on the two-year note.
At those levels, "We should see some interest and people will put money back into (Treasury) securities," Coats said.

Coats noted that the yield curve steepened a bit, as steepning trades were put on this morning. He said the two-year bond has done better than the long end since it "is a good place to hide" money in a bear market.
The market now awaits the results of the Treasury's $19.25 billion year-bill auction, which is expected to come at an average rate of 5.31 percent.
One bill trader at a Japanese bank said that the auction should go well, since year-bills are cheap to the rest of the bill sector.
The when-issued year-bill was at 5.305 just prior to the 1300 EST/1800 GMT bidding deadline.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867
